generatedProse.concept-context: Getting the most out of a placement across the School of Sport is a matter of initiative across three phases. Before you start, prepare: set your aims, read up on the setting, and agree with your supervisor how they can help. While you are there, engage: volunteer for real work, ask why a method or protocol was chosen, watch how experienced practitioners work with athletes, players or clients, and seek feedback early. Afterwards, consolidate: record what you did and learned, and connect it to your development and your applications. A coaching student, a physiologist and a sports therapist use the same three phases, even though the daily work differs.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport coaching students spend a term on the same placement with a community football club.

Tom waits to be given jobs and does them well enough: setting out cones, running the drills he is handed. When a session plan is unclear, Tom guesses rather than asks, and never requests feedback for fear of seeming unsure. The work passes, but no one stretches him, and the placement ends much as it began.

Amara asks, on the first day, what would make the term useful to the coaching staff, and volunteers to lead part of a session, just beyond her current skill. When a drill's purpose is unclear, she checks early; after each session, she asks the lead coach what could be stronger. By the end, Amara has coached harder work, learned faster, and is remembered when a reference is needed.

Same club, same length. Amara took the initiative that turned time into learning.
generatedProse.summary: You get the most out of a School of Sport placement by being proactive across three phases: preparing and aiming before, taking initiative and seeking feedback during, and recording and connecting afterwards. You can now apply these strategies, tell a proactive approach from a passive one, and choose an active move when you are in the thick of it. The last lesson is about showing what all this produced: how practice is assessed, and how to evidence your learning.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's term at the club more productive than Tom's?

items.text: She took the initiative: asking, volunteering to lead, and seeking feedback early.
She was given easier drills that were simpler to run.
She avoided asking questions so as not to seem unsure.
She waited to be told exactly what to do at each step.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara took the initiative, asking, volunteering and seeking feedback, which turned the term into learning.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara did rather than waited for.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara's term was more productive because she took the initiative: asking, volunteering to lead and seeking feedback early, rather than waiting, playing safe or guessing.
